issues.legal_issue: An allotment order made after the prescribed period is not invalid solely because of the delay when the landlord has not exercised the resulting right to nominate a tenant.
material_facts: The landlord notified the authority of the vacancy and sought release of the accommodation for personal use under Rule 6.
The allotment order was made two days after the thirty-day period had expired, while the landlord's release claim had not yet been disposed of.
The landlord did not nominate a tenant after the period expired.
issues.conclusion: The allotment order was not invalid merely because it was made after the thirty-day period; the landlord, having made no nomination, could not challenge it solely on that ground.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 7(1) and 7(2) of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, read with Rules 3, 4 and 6 of the Control of Rent and Eviction Rules, 1949, give the landlord a right to nominate a tenant when no timely allotment notice is received, but do not make a later allotment automatically void. A landlord who does not exercise the nomination right cannot attack a later allotment on timing alone. The Court relied on Jiwan Singh v. Rajindra Prasad for the consequences of the landlord's statutory duties and referred to Murlidhar Aggarwal v. State of Uttar Pradesh on the public-policy purpose of the Act.

predicates.challenge_to_allotment_order: A party challenges an order allotting accommodation under a statutory rent-control scheme.
predicates.allotment_made_after_required_window: The authority makes the allotment after the period prescribed for making it has expired.
predicates.landlord_did_not_nominate_tenant: After the prescribed period expired, the landlord did not exercise the available right to nominate a tenant.
predicates.delay_alone_does_not_void_allotment: The allotment is not invalid solely because it was made after the prescribed period.

issues.definition: When an allotment is challenged as late and the landlord did not nominate a tenant after the prescribed period, the delay alone does not void the allotment.

issues.legal_issue: A compromise that transfers control over statutory letting from the designated authority to private parties is void on public-policy grounds, and an allottee does not commit fraud by relying on the statutory process while disregarding that compromise.
material_facts: The landlord sued the allottee to challenge the allotment order, and the parties entered into a compromise under which the landlord could use the accommodation and the allottee would not enforce the allotment in specified circumstances.
The compromise also purported to give the allottee a preference if the landlord later let the accommodation.
The designated authority was not a party to the suit or compromise.
The allottee later applied for eviction and possession under the statutory procedure without relying on the compromise.
issues.conclusion: The compromise was void under section 23 of the Contract Act because it unlawfully curtailed the designated authority's control over letting; the allottee committed no fraud by ignoring it when seeking possession under section 7A.
issues.legal_principle: Section 23 of the Contract Act renders an agreement unlawful when it is opposed to public policy. Under sections 7 and 7A of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, and Rules 3 to 6 of the Control of Rent and Eviction Rules, 1949, control over letting rested with the designated authority, not the landlord and allottee. An agreement that curtails that statutory control is unlawful. The Court also relied on the public-policy rationale described in Murlidhar Aggarwal v. State of Uttar Pradesh.

predicates.challenge_to_eviction_order: A party challenges an order made in a statutory proceeding to recover accommodation from an occupant.
predicates.compromise_shifts_statutory_allocation_c: The landlord and allottee make a compromise that purports to determine who may occupy or receive the accommodation instead of leaving that control with the designated authority.
predicates.allottee_seeks_possession_through_statut: The allottee seeks possession by applying the statutory procedure for enforcing an allotment.
predicates.void_compromise_can_be_ignored_without_f: The allottee does not commit fraud by disregarding the unlawful compromise when seeking possession through the statutory process.

issues.definition: When a compromise transfers statutory allocation control to private parties and the allottee seeks possession through the statutory process, the compromise can be disregarded without that conduct being fraud.

issues.legal_issue: An allotment order is not invalid merely because a different authorized officer formally issued it when the competent delegate made the decision judicially after hearing the parties and applying his mind.
material_facts: An authorized Additional District Magistrate heard the parties and made the allotment decision after applying his mind.
An authorized Rent Controller issued the formal allotment order reflecting that decision.
issues.conclusion: The formal issuance of the order by the Rent Controller did not invalidate the allotment because the competent Additional District Magistrate had made the decision after hearing the parties and applying his mind.
issues.legal_principle: Under the Act, the Additional District Magistrate acting as a delegate of the District Magistrate and the Rent Controller were authorized to make allotment orders. The Court treated the decision as quasi-judicial and distinguished a formal issuance reflecting a competent authority's decision from an order mechanically made by an authority acting on the direction of an unauthorized body.

predicates.challenge_to_allotment_order: A party challenges the validity of an order allotting accommodation.
predicates.authorized_decision_maker_heard_parties_: An officer authorized to decide the allotment hears the parties and independently considers the matter before deciding it.
predicates.formal_issuer_recorded_the_decision: A different authorized officer issues the formal document recording the decision already made by the decision-maker.
predicates.formal_issuance_by_another_authorized_of: The allotment is not invalid merely because another authorized officer formally issued the order.

issues.definition: When an authorized decision-maker hears the parties and applies his mind, another authorized officer's formal issuance of that decision does not invalidate the allotment.

issues.legal_issue: A party seeking discretionary eviction relief must disclose a material consent decree bearing on the authority's discretion, even if the party considers the decree void.
material_facts: The allottee had entered into a consent decree recognizing the landlord's right to occupy the accommodation and restricting enforcement of the allotment order.
The allottee later sought eviction and possession without disclosing the consent decree to the authority.
The eviction authority had discretion to decline relief if eviction was inexpedient.
issues.conclusion: In the dissenting opinion, Justice Bhagwati would have held that nondisclosure of the consent decree vitiated the eviction order because the decree was material to the authority's discretion, even if it was void.
issues.legal_principle: A party seeking discretionary relief must act in good faith and disclose all known material facts bearing on the authority's discretion. Justice Bhagwati applied that principle to administrative proceedings and reasoned that a consent decree remains binding unless set aside by the appropriate process; a party cannot simply decide for itself to disregard it. He relied on Order XXIII, rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure, Wentworth v. Bullen, and United States v. United Mine Workers of America. This was the dissenting view; the majority held that the compromise was void and that ignoring it was not fraud.

predicates.application_for_discretionary_eviction_r: A party applies to an authority for eviction relief that the authority may grant or refuse in its discretion.
predicates.applicant_knows_of_material_consent_decr: The applicant knows of a consent decree that may affect whether the authority should grant eviction relief.
predicates.applicant_does_not_disclose_it: The applicant omits the consent decree from the information presented to the authority.
predicates.nondisclosure_vitiates_discretionary_evi: The resulting eviction order is vitiated because the authority was not given a material fact bearing on its discretion.

issues.definition: Under the dissenting view, nondisclosure of a known material consent decree vitiates an order granting discretionary eviction relief.
